title: 'I had no hand in causing his death': Inquest into immigration detainee's death hears SIU interview with officer
subtitle: The inquest into Abdurahman Ibrahim Hassan's death heard contradictory evidence presented by two subject officers at the scene whether the man in CBSA custody was threatened with taser and struck in the head.
article: A police officer present in the final, chaotic moments of an immigration detainee's life said he was constantly watching the restrained man's eyes and monitoring his breathing while putting a towel over his mouth to subdue him.

In an audio recording played to a jury Wednesday, late OPP Const. Andy Eberhardt was heard telling Ontario Special Investigations Unit investigators that he did not resort to any other use of force in his dealings with Abdurahman Ibrahim Hassan on the night of June 10, 2015, and the following morning.

The assertion contradicted what Peterborough police Const. Alicia McGriskin told the inquest as it began this week - that Eberhardt had threatened to taser the man who was in custody in the Peterborough Regional Health Centre and was seen striking Hassan's head on two occasions that day.

The 15-day inquest is meant to review the circumstances of Hassan's death in order to avoid such incidents in future. The coroner's counsel has suggested the cause could have been cardiac arrhythmia related to schizophrenia and antipsychotic medication, physical struggle and restraints, or asphyxia.

Eberhardt, who passed away in 2018, and McGriskin were both on paid duty that night to guard the Somali migrant, who had a history of mental health issues . Hassan had been taken to the hospital after suffering seizures at Central East Correctional Centre, a maximum-security facility in Lindsay where he was being held pending deportation.
The two police constables were named subject officers in the investigation of Hassan's death by the SIU, which reviews civilian deaths and injuries involving police officers.
Both were cleared of wrongdoing in July 2016.
In the rare disclosure of an SIU interview with a subject officer, Eberhardt is heard saying he could see a problem coming after taking a peek at Hassan from outside his hospital room.
He would later put in his police notebook: "I have never met a more vile human being."

"I was this close, gentlemen, to picking up my cellphone, saying, 'I don't want to be here.' I can read people. Within five seconds, I knew this was going to be a trouble," the OPP officer told two SIU investigators during the interview on Sept. 2, 2015.
"He was mumbling, yelling, screaming, carrying on incoherently. He certainly wasn't calm, laying there subdued."

At one point that evening, Eberhardt said, he heard a bang in Hassan's room and went in to give the patient some water with a straw. When he was leaving the room, Hassan started spitting at him and threw a styrofoam cup at the door, he added.

Later that night, according to Eberhardt, Hassan was seen picking his diaper and smearing feces over the electric controls on the side of his bed, across his face and forehead, pulling his hair and eating his excrement-laced hair.

Shortly after 10:30 p.m., five nurses and three hospital security guards, along with the two police officers, entered the tiny room to try to clean up Hassan and tighten his restraints to make sure his wrists and ankles were secured to the bed despite the man's resistance.

"I was handed a towel to wrap around his mouth for the sole purpose of preventing grievous bodily harm and injury. ... There was no upper body restraint, so I used the towel to hold down his head to prevent him from moving side to side," Eberhardt told the SIU.
"This towel was across his mouth. He was fighting around the top of the towel. He was still breathing and snorting through his mouth."
After a nurse successfully injected Hassan with a sedative, everyone left the room before returning to clean up around 1 a.m.

Eberhardt said he advised against the nurses entering the room so they "don't prod a sleeping bear," but to no avail. The two officers returned to the room with four nurses and a struggle with Hassan ensued in a similar fashion. The OPP officer said he was handed a towel by nurses.
"There is no way you could possibly hold this man's head down with your hands in rubber gloves because he was sweating and covered in excrement," Eberhardt said. "A towel is the only way to do it."

When Hassan was seen to have quickly stopped biting and moving his head, the officer said, he let go of the towel and saw the man - then naked while being cleaned and changed - urinating and stopped moving.

"I did not use any other use of force options. I did not shoot him. I did not use my taser. He was restrained. I didn't use pepper spray. I didn't use handcuffs. I had to think outside the box and using (sic) a towel like this to prevent him from spitting and biting," Eberhardt said. "I had no hand in causing his death."

During the taped interview that lasted one hour and 23 minutes, Eberhardt did not reference any threat to taser Hassan or hitting the man's head. Neither was the officer prompted by the SIU investigators about that.

However, during her testimony earlier this week, McGriskin told the inquest that Eberhardt threatened to taser Hassan when they entered the room shortly after 10:30 p.m. He also struck the side of the man's head during both confrontations, she said.

Under cross-examination by James Girvin, counsel for Eberhardt on behalf of the officer's widowed partner Mary Fice, McGriskin acknowledged she had described both the alleged threat of taser use and the head strikes for the first time in 2021 during her interview by inquest investigators.
The information was not included in her notes that were provided to the SIU or during an earlier interview by the coroner's office in 2017, she testified, because she didn't think it was relevant.
"The reason why there's no reference to strikes in your notes on either alleged occasion is because that did not occur. Would you agree or disagree with that?" Girvin asked.
"I strongly disagree," McGriskin replied.
"Would you agree or disagree with the fact that, in relation to the taser, the suggestion that that did not occur, because if it had, it would have been in your notes?" he asked.
"I strongly disagree," she again responded.
Later, when she was cross-examined by her own counsel, Joseph Markson, McGriskin denied she was doing "a favour" to Eberhardt by excluding those observations from her notes.

On Wednesday, before playing the SIU recording, coroner Dr. David Eden cautioned the five inquest jurors that they did not have the benefit of being able to cross-examine Eberhardt in order to assess the reliability of his evidence. However, they must take it into account and decide what weight to give to his testimony, Eden said.
The inquest resumes Thursday.
